questions.title: Placement does not determine synchrony
questions.prompt: The rollout engine is a separate vLLM server and the trainer is another process. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is **B**.

Placement asks **where** roles execute; synchrony asks **when** generation and updates are allowed to proceed. A separate server can still participate in a strict batch-barrier loop. Disaggregation also neither removes policy lag nor guarantees lower total memory, because state may be duplicated across pools.

options.text: The system is asynchronous by definition.
It may remain synchronous if the trainer waits for the whole batch and the next generation phase starts only after the update.
Disaggregation guarantees a smaller total cluster-memory peak.

questions.title: Logical full-training memory
questions.prompt:
A model has 7 billion parameters. The profile uses 2 bytes for each model parameter, 2 bytes for its gradient, and 8 bytes for the two Adam moments. There is no master copy.

Compute the logical full-training state:

1. in decimal GB;
2. in binary GiB.

Round GiB to two decimal places.
questions.explanation:
Each trainable parameter uses

$$
2+2+8=12\ \text{bytes}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
7\cdot10^9\cdot12
=
84\cdot10^9\ \text{bytes}
=
84.00\ \text{GB}.
$$

In GiB,

$$
\frac{84\cdot10^9}{2^{30}}
\approx78.23\ \text{GiB}.
$$

This is a logical model-state ledger. Activations, communication buffers, fragmentation, and temporary full-parameter materialization are excluded.

questions.title: KV cache for long responses
questions.explanation:
Use

$$
B_{\mathrm{KV}}
=
2L H_{\mathrm{kv}}d_hN_{\mathrm{tok}}b.
$$

The retained-token count is

$$
N_{\mathrm{tok}}=16\cdot8192=131072.
$$

Thus,

$$
B_{\mathrm{KV}}
=
2\cdot32\cdot8\cdot128\cdot131072\cdot2
=
17179869184\ \text{bytes}
=
16\ \text{GiB}.
$$

The leading factor two accounts for keys and values.

questions.title: Two architectural axes
Pipeline fill and drain
questions.explanation:
Sequential time is

$$
t_{\mathrm{seq}}
=
n(G+T)
=
8\cdot75
=
600\ \text{s}.
$$

The ideal two-stage pipeline takes

$$
t_{\mathrm{pipe}}
=
G+T+(n-1)\max(G,T)
=
45+30+7\cdot45
=
390\ \text{s}.
$$

Hence,

$$
\frac{600}{390}\approx1.538.
$$

This assumes independent resources and omits communication, queues, and duration variance.

questions.title: A straggling response
questions.prompt:
Four rollouts run concurrently for 4, 4, 4, and 12 seconds. The batch closes only after the slowest rollout.

Compute useful utilization of the four-worker capacity.
questions.explanation:
Useful work is

$$
4+4+4+12=24\ \text{worker-seconds}.
$$

Capacity available before the barrier is

$$
4\cdot12=48\ \text{worker-seconds}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
U=\frac{24}{48}=0.5.
$$

Half of the capacity is lost while workers wait for the slow response; a mean duration alone hides this loss.

questions.title: First queue check
questions.prompt:
A queue receives 8 thousand tokens per second on average, while the trainer processes 10 thousand tokens per second.

1. Compute $\rho=\lambda/\mu$.
2. Does the system pass the first-order stability check?
3. Why does this not guarantee short delays?
questions.explanation:
We obtain

$$
\rho=\frac{8}{10}=0.8.
$$

Because $\rho<1$, mean service capacity exceeds mean arrival rate and the first-order check passes.

It is not a latency guarantee. Bursts, correlated long completions, heavy tails, synchronization pauses, and bounded buffers can still create large queues. Measure the age distribution and enforce explicit backpressure.

questions.title: Effective sample size
questions.prompt:
Importance weights for four rollouts are $(1,1,1,5)$.

Compute:

1. ESS;
2. normalized ESS.

Round to four decimal places.
questions.explanation:
Use

$$
\mathrm{ESS}
=
\frac{(\sum_iw_i)^2}{\sum_iw_i^2}.
$$

The weight sum is 8 and the sum of squares is 28:

$$
\mathrm{ESS}
=
\frac{64}{28}
=
\frac{16}{7}
\approx2.2857.
$$

Normalized ESS is

$$
\frac{2.2857}{4}
=
\frac47
\approx0.5714.
$$

This diagnoses weight concentration; it does not prove absence of bias.

questions.title: Version age
questions.explanation:
The lags are

$$
(112-108,\ 112-109,\ 112-110,\ 112-110)
=
(4,3,2,2).
$$

Their mean is

$$
\bar L=\frac{4+3+2+2}{4}=2.75,
$$

and the maximum is 4. This metric requires a monotone, unambiguous version scheme; one scalar is insufficient for branched runs.

questions.title: Checkpoint interval
questions.prompt:
Writing a checkpoint takes $C=120$ s and the mean time between failures in the simplified model is $M=8$ hours.

Using Young's formula

$$
I^*=\sqrt{2CM},
$$

compute the interval in seconds and minutes.
questions.explanation:
Convert eight hours:

$$
M=8\cdot3600=28800\ \text{s}.
$$

Then

$$
I^*
=
\sqrt{2\cdot120\cdot28800}
\approx2629.07\ \text{s}
\approx43.82\ \text{min}.
$$

This is a first-order approximation. Recovery time, multilevel storage, correlated failures, and asynchronous writes change the practical policy.

questions.title: Zero lag but nonzero mismatch
questions.prompt:
Rollout and trainer recomputation use the same weight version, so policy lag is zero. Sequence log-probabilities still differ.

Name at least four possible causes and give the correct diagnostic order.

questions.title: Which rollout can be accepted
questions.explanation:
The record must not be accepted automatically. A weight version does not fully determine the behavior policy: tokenization, templating, and decoding matter. Without a verifier version, reward provenance is unknown; without stop semantics, bootstrap targets and masks cannot be reconstructed safely.

Reject or quarantine the record. Recover fields only from an immutable authoritative log, then rerun schema validation. Filling them from the current configuration would silently rewrite history.
